second_order: playing and working out Blizzard's joke mutation
theme_note: These codes share the practice of turning Blizzard's April Fools co-op mutation into a playable problem: members identify its rules, compare rushes and counters, troubleshoot rollout and rewards, and evaluate whether it is fun or frustrating. What varies is the work being done, from tactical advice and technical diagnosis to praise, criticism, and reports of successful clears.

second_order: asking Blizzard to keep the joke mutation
theme_note: These codes share a distinct practice of treating a temporary joke mode as worth preserving and directly asking Blizzard to retain or repeat it. The requests vary between wanting the altered rules permanently and wanting the event available again after April Fools.

second_order: staging, spotting, and judging April Fools jokes
theme_note: These codes belong together because participants make joke announcements, test whether surprising claims are pranks, play along, and judge whether deception is funny or in poor taste. Variation lies in who controls the joke and its consequences: some invite playful participation, while others cause hurt, worry, correction, or skepticism about genuine news.

second_order: welcoming a facts maker back without pressing him
theme_note: These codes share the practice of responding to a returning community contributor with care: accepting that he left for his happiness, offering reposting or credit arrangements, and welcoming participation on his terms. What varies is whether support takes the form of emotional reassurance, practical help, or protection of authorship.

second_order: choosing what to draw and finding room for it
theme_note: These codes share the practice of making a StarCraft presence drawable on a crowded canvas: proposing logos and characters, simplifying for legibility, comparing alternatives, locating free space, and revising the design to fit. The variation is between representational choice, feasibility judgments, and site-finding, including appeals that begin with neighboring Blizzard imagery.

second_order: rallying helpers around one plan and its coordinates
theme_note: These codes share the coordinating practice of turning interest into synchronized participation by recruiting helpers, circulating the current guide or location, moving discussion to Discord or streams, and correcting confusion about which plan is active. What varies is the coordination channel and scale, from a single invitation or link to cross-time-zone instructions and integration coordinates.

second_order: putting pixels in place and keeping the art there
theme_note: These codes share hands-on upkeep of the communal image: placing and checking pixels, repairing damage, handing maintenance between regions, defending the logo or zergling, and asking others to keep watching after completion. Variation runs from initial construction and template-following to five-minute cooldown coordination, anti-bot objections, emergency restoration, and last-pixel repair.

second_order: trading border help and making alliances
theme_note: These codes share the reciprocal practice of securing the artwork through relationships with neighboring groups: offering space or labor, arranging protection, defining borders, entering one another's Discords, and calling those exchanges alliances. What varies is formality and reach, from one-off favors and hosted work to named pacts, ambassadors, mutual maintenance, and help for third-party builds.

These codes share a governance practice: participants identify who is organizing, route questions or diplomacy to those people, centralize scattered posts, and approve or update changes through an informal decision process. What varies is the claimed authority—majority preference, practical leadership, ambassador work, or explicit reminders that organizers are not subreddit moderators.

second_order: working out overlaps without wrecking neighbors
theme_note: These codes share the practice of handling collisions while trying to limit damage: diagnosing overlapping plans, negotiating turns or boundaries, yielding space, warning against retaliation, and distinguishing repair from attack. Variation includes tense blame and ignored deals as well as restraint, apology, accommodation, and explicit refusal to consume another project.

second_order: calling it done and retelling how it held
theme_note: These codes share the practice of marking collective accomplishment and turning the finished canvas into community memory: announcing completion, thanking contributors and allies, mourning the ending, locating landmarks, explaining the event to late readers, and narrating which images survived. What varies is temporal position and tone, from mid-event 'we did it' claims and jokes about rivals to post-event celebration, explanation, coincidence-spotting, and recollection of the last repair or a restrained pixel tug.

second_order: arguing over spreading creep across other work
theme_note: These codes share one bounded dispute about extending a StarCraft creep-colony motif into occupied canvas space. Participants vary between treating expansion and conversion as playful faction competition, preferring an old-school design, and rejecting overwriting or retaliation as a dick move that threatens the existing logo.
